title: DOD releases 1956 report outlining UFO encounter over Guam
excerpt: The Department of Defense last week released a confidential 1956 Air Force Air Intelligence Information Report that outlines an encounter between an Air Force fighter-interceptor aircraft and an unidentified flying
content:
The Department of Defense last week released a confidential 1956 Air Force Air Intelligence Information Report that outlines an encounter between an Air Force fighter-interceptor aircraft and an unidentified flying object over Guam.

DOD said the intelligence report was a standardized Air Force reporting form used to record raw information of potential intelligence value for later analysis throughout the early Cold War.

It noted that all descriptions and estimations in the report are the reporter’s “subjective interpretation at the time of the event.”

The disclosure was part of the latest tranche of records related to UFOs, or UAPs, unidentified anomalous phenomena, released by the DOD this year. President Donald Trump in May signed an executive order mandating the disclosure of the sensitive files.

Blinking light in the sky

According to the report, the incident over Guam took place during the evening of Dec. 31, 1956. A pilot of an Air Force F-86D Sabre reported observing an unidentified aerial blinking light.

The pilot, 1st Lt. Ted Brunson of the 41st Fighter-Interceptor Squadron, was flying in a holding pattern above the island at about 20,000 feet above sea level where he observed a round, white, dime-sized object from his cockpit.

The object emitted a solid white light, which periodically blinked very quickly.

Brunson observed the object passed under his aircraft and initially mistook it for a B-47 Stratojet bomber. He turned to intercept it.

The object began turning with Brunson’s aircraft, and the pilot grew suspicious because no other fighter aircraft were airborne at that time and no other local aircraft could turn as sharply as his F-86D interceptor jet.

Later, the object traveled south for about 10 miles at 20,000 feet before climbing to about 30,000 feet. It then came directly over Brunson’s aircraft and began circling him.

He put his jet into afterburner and turned into the object to try and cut it off but was unable to get any closer, the report stated.

The object headed west and circled his aircraft again at 10,000 to 15,000 feet. With fuel running low, Brunson broke off his pursuit and returned to Andersen Air Force Base where contact with the object was lost.

The encounter lasted roughly 10 minutes, according to the report.

A decade ago, Brunson’s son recalled an incident involving his father that seems to match the details of the report released last week. However, Brunson’s son dated the incident for New Year’s Day 1957.

Reports of UFOs in Guam’s skies have not been uncommon over the years.

Air Force looks at ballon

According to the 1956 report, the Air Force was advised to check on any lighted balloons that might have been released around the time of the sighting, since the UFO sighting was similar to sightings of weather balloons.

They received confirmation that a lighted ballon was launched by the U.S. Weather Bureau, now National Weather Service, about an hour and 38 minutes before the reported encounter from the U.S. Navy Communication’s Station.

It was last tracked five miles west of the station at an altitude of 20,000 feet about an hour and 10 minutes before the encounter.

Brunson was questioned but stated he did not believe the UFO was a weather balloon because, “the [UFO] maneuvered with the F-86D and accelerated past his aircraft.”

Air Force Capt. Alan Pound, the Air Tech Intel Liaison Officer who prepared the report, noted that the check on the lighted weather balloon’s ascension rate was somewhat slower than a typical weather balloon.

“If the weather balloon had ascended normally, it would have been much higher than the altitude of the reported sighting,” Pound wrote. “If the balloon had malfunctioned and leveled off or descended, it could possibly explain the reported [UFO].”

However, Pound noted that the ballon explanation was not sufficient, unless a record of a malfunction was recorded.
